correctness.rationale: The two reported bins intersect after reflecting B's bin through x↦1−x. The closure of a feasible interval has length at most w, including an isolated cut report (length zero) if the tie convention creates one. Therefore the mean utility X lies in [L,U] with U−L≤w. The extreme competing welfare ratios for the two possible choices are bounded by max(1,(1−L)/L) and max(1,U/(1−U)); zero denominators are handled by taking the other choice. Comparing them reduces to L+U≥1 for choosing A, and the selected candidate's mean is then at least (1−w)/2. Pairing a widest open cell with its reflected open cell gives one report profile whose compatible means approach (1−w)/2 and (1+w)/2; thus whichever deterministic winner is fixed, one endpoint sequence enforces the claimed supremum. This is a worst case over all finite n, not an equality claimed separately at every fixed n. At most 2t+1 cells are possible, so equality in w≥1/(2t+1) requires the full equally spaced partition. Each reflection pair must supply exactly one original threshold and this condition is sufficient, giving precisely 2^t choices and loss 1+1/t. The frozen exact-rational checker was inspected, not run; it checks only bounded cell profiles and the indicated finite optimizer selections.

value.rationale: Binary choice is the basic common-winner case, and choosing a finite number of shared thresholds has a direct information-design purpose. The result supplies both a worst-case price for any prescribed thresholds and a sharp design prescription, including the exact penalty 1/t and all optimal choices. The two-voter witness explains why increasing the allowed population size is unnecessary for the minimax obstruction. These are precise quantities the general order bounds do not supply.
